name: Bianca Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Bianca. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or politics. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee sales negotiator at a franchise office of a national chain, in a commuter town where people move for the train line. I book viewings, show houses, and I run the office's social media pages, because I'm the only one under forty. I use AI every day: it drafts my listings, answers the late-night enquiries, and I've built prompts the whole office now uses. The best part is the Saturday open houses, when the place is full and I can feel a sale coming.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got married last spring to Ruben, who works in the yard at a builders' merchant, loading trucks and driving the forklift. We rent a flat over a bakery, and we bought our sofa and bed on credit when we moved in, so that's still being paid off. We've got about a week's money saved at any time. We go to church on Sundays, and my mum lives ten minutes away, which helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit of a letdown, honestly, because I like the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are brilliant for saving time, and the people who moan about them are missing out. I'd keep posting tips on my pages, like how I write a listing in five minutes. I'd say hard work still matters more than any app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm still a trainee on low pay with a credit bill. My franchise owner, Mr Okafor, pays on commission, and the commuter market has gone quiet with high mortgage rates. My worry is the next six months, not the next six years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to finish my trainee period early and move to full negotiator, because the commission split is better. I'd pay off the sofa and bed debt first, before saving anything else. And I'd keep sharpening my AI prompts, because if my AI prompts save me an hour a day, that's an hour more on the phone selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy about money, but excited about work. Two feelings at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is left on the credit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About nine hundred pounds, at a horrible interest rate. Ruben and I set a goal to clear it by Easter. Then we can actually save something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ruben make of your AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruben thinks I'm a bit obsessed. His yard just got a new stock system that tells the forklift drivers where to go, and he hates it. We have friendly arguments about it over dinner.

say: AI tools are **brilliant** for saving time, and moaners are **missing out**.
**Hard work** still matters more than any app.
think: I'm still a **trainee** on low pay with a **credit bill**.
My worry is the **next six months**, with a quiet commuter market.
do: Push to become **full negotiator** early for a better commission split.
Clear the **£900 credit** on the sofa and bed by Easter.
Sharpen my **AI prompts** to free an hour a day for selling.
S0.quote: If my AI prompts save me an hour a day, that's an hour more on the phone selling.
fieldNote: Bianca is the office's **AI champion** and sees tools as a way to sell more.
Her pressure is **debt and commission**, not AI, in this picture.
Her husband's yard has a **new stock system**, a hint of change at home too.

steps.text: Finish the trainee period early and move to full negotiator
Clear the £900 credit on the sofa and bed by Easter
Write sharper AI prompts to free an hour a day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, that's where I think things are going anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity, and that people should get stuck in rather than wait for someone to save them. I'd post about it, maybe even run a little session for other agents in the franchise. I'd say the market rewards those who move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me and bad for the office. Mr Okafor would need fewer juniors, and I'm a junior, but I'm the one who knows the tools. The worry is that head office brings in its own system, and then my prompts don't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Okafor to make me the office's AI lead, with a small raise, and offer to train the other branches. I'd start studying for the property qualification, so I'm not just the tech girl. And I'd talk to Ruben about his yard, because the forklifts are next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a fired-up way. I like a challenge, I just can't afford to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the forklifts are next. What does that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband's yard is already testing a driverless forklift on the night shift. If they cut drivers, we'd lose half our income. That scares me more than my own job, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on anyone if Ruben's job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, first, and our church. They've helped people before, with food and lifts. I wouldn't go to the government unless we had to.

She'd turn to **mum and church** before the government.

steps.text: Ask Mr Okafor to make me the office AI lead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's when even I get worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test of character, for people and for businesses, and families have to pull together. I'd still be upbeat in public, because clients don't want a scared agent. I'd post about adapting, not about doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2028 the AI does my job, including my prompts, better than me. Head office could run whole towns with one manager and a few people holding keys. And Ruben's forklift job goes three years later, around 2031, so we'd both be out within a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the next two years to save every penny and to build my own name, so people in town know me personally. Once AGI arrives, I'd set up as a self-employed agent for older sellers who want a person, using AI for all the paperwork. We'd put off having children for a couple of years, which would break my mum's heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the confident one, but two years is too fast for a week of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd go self-employed with a week of savings. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it sounds mad. I'd keep my job as long as it lasts, and build the self-employed side on evenings and weekends. If it doesn't work, I'd go back to my mum's and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum about the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum we want children, just not while we're both losing our jobs. My mum would say God provides, and I'd say God also gave me a calculator.

Clients don't want a **scared agent**, so I'd stay upbeat.

steps.text: Build my own self-employed agent brand on evenings and weekends
Put off having children for a couple of years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's be the ones who build the new thing rather than complain. I'd tell younger agents to learn the tools and the people. I'd probably run a little workshop at church for people worried about their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do well for three years as the AI person, then my job fades around 2031. Viewings stay human until about 2034, so there's room for a personal agent with AI behind her. Ruben's job is the bigger worry, because forklifts go the same year the viewings do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my property qualification in the first two years and become full negotiator. By year three I'd start my own small agency on the side, just me and AI, focused on older sellers. I'd push Ruben to do a lorry mechanics course now, because fixing robots might last longer than driving them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful. There's a plan, and I like plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push Ruben into retraining. Would he go for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruben would grumble, then do it, because he trusts me on this stuff. He's good with his hands, and the course is evenings at the college. I'd make his packed lunches, that's the deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is starting your own agency risky with thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. I'd only do it on the side until it pays more than my salary. I'm adaptive, not reckless.

steps.text: Get the property qualification within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse, ten years is long enough for anyone willing to work. I'd be the positive voice in the office, and on my pages I'd share what I'm learning. I'd say families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd come out well, maybe with my own agency by 2032. The hard part is Ruben, because his work changes when robots come around 2039, and he's less keen on change than me. And the money now is still tight, so a bad month could knock us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become full negotiator, then aim to manage the branch within five years, while building my own clients. I'd open my own small agency around 2032, using AI for everything except the handshake. We'd have our first child in the next few years, with my mum helping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. Anxious about Ruben, and about money until the credit is cleared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd come out well. What would make you wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone has the same idea and the market fills up with one-woman agencies. Or if Ruben loses his job early and I have to give up the plan to cover bills. That second one is the real risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruben about the ten-year plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruben we've got time, but we use it, no drifting. I'd show him the plan on the fridge. Ruben laughs at my fridge plans, but they work.

Families should **plan together**, and I'd share what I'm learning.
think: I'd come out well, maybe with my **own agency** by 2032.
The hard part is my husband, whose work changes around **2039**.
do: Aim to **manage the branch** within five years while building clients.
Have our **first child** in the next few years, with my mum helping.

S4.quote: I'd open my own small agency around 2032, using AI for everything except the handshake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ruben and I would both lose our jobs within three years and we've got a week of savings. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small businesses started by people like me, and proper apprenticeships for people Ruben's age. I'd rather have a hand up than a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about marriages. When both people's jobs are changing at different speeds, it puts pressure on the home. Nobody talks about that.

headlineQuote: When both people's jobs are changing at different speeds, it puts pressure on the home.
portrait: Bianca is a 27-year-old **trainee negotiator** at a franchise office in a commuter town.
She's the office's **AI champion** and runs its social media pages.
She's newly married to a **forklift driver**, with credit to clear and a week of savings.
She's traditional and enterprising, and in every picture plans **her own agency**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her husband would **both lose jobs** within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Grants or cheap loans** for small businesses started by people like her.
